Overview/Pied-à-terre checker/Tax list

Pied-à-terre tax · FY2027 Roll

Is there a pied-à-terre tax list?

About 8,000 New York City properties were billed for the second-home surcharge. Here is what is public about them, and how to see where a building stands.

The most common rising search about the surcharge is some form of "pied-à-terre tax list". Owners, buyers and managing agents want to know whether their building, or a building they are looking at, is on it.

What the city has done

In July 2026 the Department of Finance sent initial notices to about 17,000 owners. After granting roughly 8,900 exemptions for primary residences and long-term rentals, it billed about 8,000 properties. The charge appears on the owner's property tax statement and is due January 1, 2027.

An owner's own notice and tax statement are the official answer for that property. Both can be looked up by address or BBL on the Department of Finance website.

What these pages show instead

This site does not publish owners or a list of who pays. It publishes building-level counts from the public FY2027 roll:

  • the building index: 661 condominiums with at least five units valued at $1 million or more, and 396 co-ops whose building value averages $1 million or more per apartment;
  • a page for each building and neighborhood hub, with the number of units over the line, the brackets they fall in, and how the city valued the building;
  • aggregate borough and ZIP counts for 1–3 family Class 1 houses over $5 million;
  • the free checker, which looks up one apartment or house by address and shows its city value and bracket.

A unit over the line is not necessarily billed. Whether the surcharge applies depends on who lives there (exemptions guide), and the assessment roll does not record occupancy.

The rules in short

  • Condos and co-ops: from a city market value of $1 million. 4% of the whole value up to $3 million, 5.25% up to $5 million, 6.5% above.
  • One- to three-family houses: from $5 million. 0.8% up to $15 million, 1.05% up to $25 million, 1.3% above.
  • Period: Phase 1 runs from July 1, 2026 to June 30, 2028. From July 1, 2028, condos and co-ops are valued from comparable sales and move to the houses' $5 million threshold and rates.
  • First bills: for values up to $50,000 above the $1 million or $5 million threshold, the first bills appear to phase the charge in rather than charge the full amount. The city Comptroller reported this in November 2026 and noted that the law contains no phase-in language.

The surcharge is not owed when the home is the primary residence of the owner, the owner's spouse, child, parent, sibling, grandparent or grandchild, or a tenant or subtenant on a bona fide arm's-length lease of at least one year. Residence is tested on the taxable status date before the fiscal year: January 5, 2026 for 2026–27. When an LLC, corporation or partnership owns the home, the people who together hold a majority interest count as owners; when a trust owns it, its sole beneficiaries do. Owning through an entity does not by itself make a home anyone's primary residence. Other exemptions and abatements do not reduce the surcharge (Tax Law § 1354(a)).

Deadline to appeal the value or residency

To contest the market value behind the surcharge, file Tax Commission Form TC107 by March 1, 2027 for condos and co-ops, or March 15, 2027 for houses. The same form appeals the Department of Finance's residency determination; if you first asked DOF to review residency, the deadline for that part is the March date or 30 days after DOF's final notice, whichever is later. The form cannot be used to protest the assessed value. See the TC107 guide or the deadline timeline.
